anxIntro: The site measures how much countries talk about the topics of UNODC's mandate in the UN General Debate. These are the steps, in brief.
s1: A total of {speeches} General Debate speeches by {countries} countries, from {first} to {last}, were gathered. Those from 1946 to 2023 and from 2025 come from the UN General Debate Corpus. Those from 2024 come from the UN's official records, and those from 2026 from a transcript of the session's audio, still provisional. All texts are in English.
s2: Each speech was split into fragments of one or a few paragraphs, of about 60 to 260 words: {all} fragments. The {ceremonial} fragments of pure protocol, such as congratulating the President or giving thanks, were set aside, leaving {fragments} for the analysis.
s3: A language model turned each fragment into a list of numbers that sums up what it says. Fragments about the same thing end up close together, even when they use different words.
s4: A sample of {labelled} fragments was drawn at random, more often where each topic was likely, so that every topic and period had examples. An AI language model read them one by one, without seeing the country or the speaker, following rules based on UNODC's official definitions, and marked the topics each fragment develops, not those it only names. It read {read} topics: {unodc} UNODC topics and {ref}, as a reference. A second, stricter AI reader read {checked} fragments again: a control sample, doubtful cases and those touched by revised rules. Where the two disagreed, a third decided.
s5: With those examples, {models} models were trained, one per UNODC topic. Each learns to recognize its topic in the fingerprint of meaning and gives each fragment a probability, from 0 to 100%. Peace and security has no model: it takes up about two fifths of the text and is better described by the general topics (step 7).
s6: The examples were split into {folds} parts, by speech. Each model was trained {folds} times on {rest} parts and scored on the part it had not seen. Those scores chose its settings and its threshold, the probability from which a fragment counts as being about the topic (the one that best balances precision and recall), and measure how well it works. The final model was trained on all the examples with those settings.
s7: Fragments about no UNODC topic were grouped by closeness of meaning into {general} general topics, named after reading examples of each. The conversation map draws each fragment's fingerprint on a plane. Each speech is placed by the average fingerprint of its fragments.
accTitle: How well does each model work?
accHint: Cross-validation on the {labelled} fragments read. Each fragment weighs by how many like it the whole corpus holds, so that the figures describe it.
accExD: Fragments read that are about the topic.
accPrec: Of every 100 fragments the model marks with the topic, how many are really about it.
accRec: Of every 100 fragments about the topic, how many the model marks.
accF1: Joins precision and recall into one figure: it drops if either is low. Each model's threshold is the one that makes it highest.
accBarNote: The tick marks {bar}: the F1 “Measured” requires overall and in every period with at least {min} examples of the topic (1946–1969, 1970–1989, 1990–2009, 2010–2024 and 2025–2026).
st_okD: Its F1 reaches {bar} or more, overall and in every period.
st_apxD: Its F1 falls short of that level overall or in some period. Its averages broadly follow the share read, but some fragments it marks belong to a neighbouring topic and others slip through. Good for seeing large changes.
useT: How the site uses the models
use1: Mandate footprint, world map and trends: the average probability of each speech's fragments, which estimates how much of the speech is about the topic. It does not depend on the threshold, so a doubtful fragment weighs little. In a group, each country weighs the same.
use2: Colours of the conversation map, words that set them apart, “What it talked about” and “What they say”: the fragments above their topic's threshold. “What they say” shows the most probable ones, in full.
use3: A fragment about {subs} also counts as being about {p}.
use4: A fragment's card (click on the map): its whole text and, for each topic, the model's hit rate at a probability like its own, that is, of every 10 such fragments, how many are about the topic in the cross-validation. If the fragment is in the read sample, it shows what the reader decided.
lim1: The 2026 speeches are provisional: they come from a transcript of the audio.
lim2: A topic mentioned in passing in a fragment about something else may be missed, and one only named in a list may be counted by mistake.
lim3: The cross-validation figures are somewhat optimistic, because the settings were chosen on the same data, and uncertain where examples are few.
lim4: The site measures what is talked about, not the position taken.
footer: Source: UN General Debate Corpus (Jankin, Baturo and Dasandi 2025; Baturo, Dasandi and Mikhaylov 2017).
